subject: Cognitive Science
title: Wisdom of Crowds
description: A quick, practical guide to Wisdom of Crowds.

hook.text: At a county fair in 1906, 800 people guessed the weight of an ox. The average guess was off by one pound.

buildup.text: Francis Galton was stunned. No individual was accurate, but the crowd's average was nearly perfect.

discovery.text: Crowd wisdom works when opinions are diverse, independent, and aggregated. Individual errors cancel out.

twist.text: But if people see each other's guesses, independence breaks. Social influence destroys crowd wisdom.

climax.text: Prediction markets work on this principle: aggregate independent bets and you get remarkably accurate forecasts.

punchline.text: A crowd of independent thinkers beats any single expert.

quiz.question: What condition is essential for crowd wisdom to work?

details.summary: When individuals make independent estimates, their average often beats experts. Galton found that a crowd's median guess of an ox's weight was nearly perfect. The wisdom of crowds requires diversity, independence, and decentralization. When these conditions fail, crowds become mobs.
details.whyItMatters: Crowd wisdom underlies prediction markets, Wikipedia, and democratic decision-making. Knowing when it works and when it fails is essential for aggregating information well.
takeaways: Averaged independent estimates often beat individual experts
Diversity, independence, and decentralization are required conditions
Social influence and herding destroy crowd accuracy

faq.question: Why does averaging independent estimates work so well?
faq.answer: Individual errors are random and cancel out when averaged. Some people guess too high, others too low. If errors are independent and unbiased, the mean converges on the truth. This only works when guesses are made without seeing others' answers and when the crowd is diverse.

faq.question: When does the wisdom of crowds fail?
faq.answer: It fails when people are not independent, as in social media echo chambers, or when information cascades cause everyone to follow early adopters. Homogeneous groups also fail because their errors are correlated rather than random. Bubbles and panics are examples of crowd folly.
